warnings: Total vitamin C from food plus supplements should stay below 2000 mg per day for adults (US NASEM; ICMR-NIN upper limit not found). Many experts suggest under 1000 mg per day from supplements (UK NHS).
Large doses can cause diarrhoea, stomach cramps and wind.
Regular vitamin C supplements have been linked with higher kidney stone risk in men; people with a history of kidney stones or with kidney disease should check with a doctor first.
People with iron-overload conditions (haemochromatosis, frequent transfusions) or G6PD deficiency should take vitamin C supplements only on medical advice.
High-dose antioxidants may interact with chemotherapy or radiotherapy, statin plus niacin treatment, warfarin, oestrogen-containing medicines and aluminium antacids; ask the doctor or pharmacist.
Vitamin C from ordinary food does not need an upper-limit warning.
General information, not medical advice. Check with a doctor before starting supplements.
Supplements of 1,000 mg/day or more can cause stomach upset and, in men, may raise kidney stone risk; gentle app notice at 1,000 mg/day from supplements
Upper limit 2,000 mg/day from food plus supplements (NASEM); ICMR-NIN TUL Not found; EFSA sets none
Kidney stone history or kidney disease: food vitamin C is fine; avoid vitamin C supplements of 1,000 mg/day or more; requires_doctor_input
Iron overload (haemochromatosis, thalassaemia major on deferoxamine): no vitamin C supplement quick-add; doses above 500 mg/day were linked to heart problems with deferoxamine; requires_doctor_input
G6PD deficiency: high-dose, especially intravenous, vitamin C has caused red-cell destruction; requires_doctor_input
Glucose sensors (CGM) and some meters and lab tests can read falsely high with vitamin C tablets (Libre 2 label: over 500 mg/day; Libre 3: over 1,000 mg/day); tell your doctor or lab
Chemotherapy or radiation, warfarin, statin plus niacin, aluminium-containing medicines: ask your doctor before vitamin C supplements
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: supplements only if a doctor advises
Vitamin C does not prevent colds in the general population; no immunity-boost claims
